newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria president warns of hard times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria president warns of hard times ahead.

text.p: President Petar Stoyanov blamed the departing ex-communist government for Bulgaria's woes on Wednesday and warned of more hard times to come.
In a television broadcast after appointing an interim cabinet led by Sofia's mayor Stefan Sofianski and setting April 19 as the date for general elections, Stoyanov said:
"Fellow countrymen, I know the situation is grave but I cannot promise that in the next month the situation will become better.

"Today our compatriots live in misery unknown to the civilised world. A misery which is not the result of people's inability to manage their destinies, but of the inability of those in power to provide better living conditions," he added.
After 30 days of mass protests, the Socialists last week gave up efforts to form a new cabinet and agreed to elections 20 months before the end of their parliamentary term.
Stoyanov said that in four years the Bulgarians had become 10 times poorer, the national currency had depreciated 100 times and domestic debt topped three trillion levs after the lev's latest slump.
Cumulative inflation from 1991 to end-1996 is 24,000 percent and wages have fallen seven times in dollar terms in the same period, he said.

With the exception of a government of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces from November 1991 to December 1992, all Bulgaria's elected cabinets since 1989 have been led by or had the support of the Socialist party.
"Once again we are back to where we started from with inadequate prices and empty (store) shelves. And again we are expecting yet another price shock," he added.

The caretaker cabinet, which will hold its first meeting on Thursday, contains several critics of the outgoing Socialist government, and abolishes the economic development portfolio created by the Socialists.
"It will be unfair to the interim government if we do not say clearly how difficult is its inheritance because it will have to pay for actions it has not committed," said Stoyanov.
"Part of the measures to be taken by the interim government will be very unpopular... that is why the cabinet will be expected to announce publicly the cause and extent of the economic crisis."

Stoyanov -- a charismatic figure although his duties as head of state are in normal times mainly ceremonial -- urged the cabinet to curb uncontrolled siphoning of funds abroad and launch criminal proceedings against those who had caused the crisis.

The caretaker cabinet must also speed up long-delayed structural reforms such as privatisation and closing loss-making state firms, cutting state spending, cracking down on corruption and the grey economy, and encouraging investment.
The International Monetary Fund and other lending organisations have said they are ready to send missions to Sofia as soon as a new government is in place.
"After the brief term of the interim government I expect that Bulgarians will be able to look at the future with more hope," said Stoyanov.
